Statistics of Income" ) ``` ::: **Observation:**\ The income distribution is heavily right-skewed, with the majority of labourers earning in the lower brackets. The long tail on the right shows that a small number earn much more than the rest, highlighting uneven earnings and suggest that income is unevenly distributed. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Visualisation 2: Income Across Socioeconomic Factors (Province, Education, Credit) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ :::: callout-note ## Visualisation 2: Income Across Socioeconomic Factors (Province, Education, Credit) ::: panel-tabset ### Visual ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](THE01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Code ``` r y_max <- quantile(df$income, 0.98, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.10 # Plot A: Income by Province df_cpro <- df %>% drop_na(income, cpro) p_cpro <- ggplot(df_cpro, aes(x = cpro, y = income)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_max)) + labs( title = "Income by Province", x = "Province", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() #Plot B: Income by Education df_fedu <- df %>% drop_na(income, fedu) p_fedu <- ggplot(df_fedu, aes(x = fedu, y = income)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_max)) + labs( title = "Income by Education Level", x = "Education Level", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() # Plot C: Income by Credit Access df_fcra <- df %>% drop_na(income, fcra) p_fcra <- ggplot(df_fcra, aes(x = fcra, y = income)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_max)) + labs( title = "Income by Credit Access", x = "Credit Access", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() # Display the combined plots p_cpro + p_fedu + p_fcra ``` ::: **Observation:**\ Income varies across provinces, education levels, and credit access categories. Education shows the clearest pattern, with higher education levels generally associated with higher median incomes. Credit access is linked to slightly higher earnings, while provincial differences are present but less pronounced. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Visualisation 3: Income Across Demographic Characteristics (Gender, Training) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ :::: callout-note ## Visualisation 3: Income Across Demographic Characteristics (Gender, Training) ::: panel-tabset ### Visual ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](THE01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} |Group |Category | N| Median_Income| Mean_Income| SD| |:-------------|:------------|---:|-------------:|-----------:|-----:| |Gender |Male | 591| 32| 38.39| 32.48| |Gender |Female | 133| 31| 36.26| 29.40| |Training type |Short course | 609| 29| 32.47| 16.46| |Training type |Long course | 92| 65| 74.98| 66.55| ::: ::: ### Code ``` r y_max <- quantile(df$income, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE) # Plot A: Income by Gender df_gender <- df %>% drop_na(income, cgen) p_gender <- ggplot(df_gender, aes(x = cgen, y = income)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_max)) + labs( title = "Income by Gender", x = "Gender", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() # Plot B: Income by Vocational Training Type df_training <- df %>% drop_na(income, fvtp) p_training <- ggplot(df_training, aes(x = fvtp, y = income)) + geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, y_max)) + labs( title = "Income by Vocational Training Type", x = "Training type", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() p_gender + p_training # 5. Summary Table summary_v3 <- bind_rows( df_gender %>% group_by(Group = "Gender", Category = cgen) %>% summarise( N = n(), Median_Income = median(income, na.rm = TRUE), Mean_Income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), SD = sd(income, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ), df_training %>% group_by(Group = "Training type", Category = fvtp) %>% summarise( N = n(), Median_Income = median(income, na.rm = TRUE), Mean_Income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), SD = sd(income, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) ) knitr::kable(summary_v3, digits = 2) ``` ::: **Observation:**\ Income differences across gender appear minimal, with considerable overlap between the two groups. In contrast, vocational training type shows a clearer gap: respondents who attended long courses report substantially higher incomes than those who attended short courses. However, variability within each group remains large, especially for the long-course group. This suggests that factors beyond gender and training type also contribute to income differences. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Visualisation 4: Association Between Income and Savings ------------------------------------------------------------------------ :::: callout-note ## Visualisation 4:Association Between Income and Savings ::: panel-tabset ### Visual ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](THE01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Summary of Income and Savings Relationship | N| Correlation_Pearson| Correlation_Spearman| Income_Mean| Savings_Mean| |---:|-------------------:|--------------------:|-----------:|------------:| | 205| 0.015| 0.403| 50.717| 44.171| ::: ::: ### Code ``` r df_scatter <- df %>% drop_na(income, lsav) x_limit <- quantile(df_scatter$income, 0.98, na.rm = TRUE) y_limit <- quantile(df_scatter$lsav, 0.98, na.rm = TRUE) ggplot(df_scatter, aes(x = income, y = lsav)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, x_limit), ylim = c(0, y_limit)) + labs( title = "Association Between Income and Savings", x = "Income (Million VND)", y = "Savings" ) + theme_minimal() # Summary table knitr::kable( df_scatter %>% summarise( N = n(), Correlation_Pearson = cor(income, lsav, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs"), Correlation_Spearman = cor(income, lsav, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"), Income_Mean = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), Savings_Mean = mean(lsav, na.rm = TRUE) ), digits = 3, caption = "Summary of Income and Savings Relationship" ) ``` ::: **Observation:**\ Savings show a weak relationship with income, with points widely dispersed and clustered at lower savings levels. A small number of extreme values influence the fitted trend line, and most respondents report relatively low savings even as income increases. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Visualisation 5: Income by Perception Score (PPO1) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ :::: callout-note ## Visualisation 5: Income by Perception Score (PPO1) ::: panel-tabset ### Visual ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](THE01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Income Summary by PPO1 Score
Scale: 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree (as defined in the survey) |ppo1 | N| Median_Income| Mean_Income| SD| |:----|---:|-------------:|-----------:|-----:| |1 | 150| 29| 35.97| 21.90| |2 | 145| 35| 37.20| 17.51| |3 | 78| 34| 41.05| 27.04| |4 | 69| 30| 45.51| 67.56| |5 | 73| 28| 40.10| 42.75| ::: ::: ### Code ``` r df_ppo1 <- df %>% mutate(ppo1 = na_if(ppo1, 0)) %>% drop_na(ppo1, income) %>% mutate(ppo1 = factor(ppo1, levels = 1:5, ordered = TRUE)) upper_limit <- quantile(df_ppo1$income, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE) ggplot(df_ppo1, aes(x = ppo1, y = income)) + geom_boxplot() + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, upper_limit)) + labs( title = "Income by PPO1 Score", x = "PPO1 score (1–5)", y = "Income (Million VND)" ) + theme_minimal() knitr::kable( df_ppo1 %>% group_by(ppo1) %>% summarise( N = n(), Median_Income = median(income, na.rm = TRUE), Mean_Income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE), SD = sd(income, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ), digits = 2, caption = "Income Summary by PPO1 Score
Scale: 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree (as defined in the survey)" ) ``` ::: **Observation:**\ PPO1 reflects respondents’ views on training-related policy/support. This visualisation explores whether income levels differ across PPO1 score categories. Income distributions overlap heavily across PPO1 score levels, and median income changes only minimally from scores 1 to 5. While the mean income is higher for some scores , the large differences indicate that a small number of high-income outliers likely drive these differences. Overall, the plot suggests no clear or strong relationship between PPO1 score and income. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Visualisation 6: Heatmap of Income Distribution by Education Level ------------------------------------------------------------------------ :::: callout-note ## Visualisation 6: Heatmap of Income Distribution by Education Level ::: panel-tabset ### Visual ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](THE01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} |Education Level | Respondents|Percentage | |:---------------|-----------:|:----------| |Primary | 473|67.5% | |Lower secondary | 136|19.4% | |Upper secondary | 73|10.4% | |Others | 19|2.7% | ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Total number of respondents (used in heatmap): 701 ``` ::: ::: ### Code ``` r df_hm <- df %>% drop_na(income, fedu) %>% mutate( income_band = ntile(income, 4), income_band = factor( income_band, levels = 1:4, labels = c("Q1 (Lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (Highest)"), ordered = TRUE ) ) # Plot Heatmap df_hm %>% count(fedu, income_band) %>% group_by(fedu) %>% mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = fedu, y = income_band, fill = pct)) + geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) + scale_fill_gradient(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) + labs( title = "Heatmap of Income Band by Education Level", x = "Education Level", y = "Income Band", fill = "% within Edu" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) # Summary Table knitr::kable( df_hm %>% count(fedu, name = "Respondents") %>% mutate(Percentage = scales::percent(Respondents / sum(Respondents), accuracy = 0.1)), col.names = c("Education Level", "Respondents", "Percentage") ) cat("Total number of respondents (used in heatmap):", nrow(df_hm)) ``` ::: **Observation:**\ The heatmap shows, within each education group, the proportion of respondents in each income quartile (Q1 = lowest income, Q4 = highest). Respondents with primary and lower secondary education are more concentrated in the lower income bands (Q1–Q2), while upper secondary and “others” show a relatively higher share in the upper bands (Q3–Q4). This pattern suggests a mild positive relationship between education attainment and income. :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ # Overall Observations Income of informal rural labourers in the northern mountainous regions of Vietnam is highly uneven and right-skewed, with most labourers clustered at lower income levels and a small group earning much more. Across the factors examined, education stands out as the strongest and most consistent correlate of income, reflected in higher medians and a greater share in upper income quartiles for more educated respondents. Credit access and vocational training type show secondary, weaker patterns , but dispersion remains large, suggesting other influences are also important. In contrast, province, gender, savings , and PPO1 show modest or minimal differentiation in income.
